newsitem.title: PERU: Peru growth could be hurt by politics - Barings.
newsitem.headline: Peru growth could be hurt by politics - Barings.

text.p: Peru is back on track this year for solid, sustained growth, but internal political problems could hinder this, said Arturo Porzecanski, managing director and chief economist of ING Barings in New York.

"Peru has now had various months of growth. If it continues like that, we are going to change our projection to 5.5 percent annual growth in 1997 from 4.5 percent initially," Porzecanski told reporters in Lima.
The Peruvian economy grew 4.8 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, compared with a 0.6 percent year-on-year growth in the January to March period of 1996.
The government estimates gross domestic product growth of four to five percent in 1997, after 2.8 percent in 1996 and 7.0 percent the previous year.
"At last inflation has fallen to one digit annually" and the fiscal deficit is coming under control, added Porzecanski, referring to Peru's annualized inflation rate of about nine percent.

Porzecanski warned, however, that "the Peruvian economy's new take-off" was not helped by recent political events. "In the political part, I see that there is a lot of noise that could distract a little investor and business attention."
He cited the debate over Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's eligibility to seek a third reelection in 2000 and the government's confrontation with the constitutional tribunal over this issue.

"I thought that after the freedom from the embassy, it was all party and peace," he said, referring to the recently-ended hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima. "But really I believe that some subjects are getting worse."

He also regretted "an important slowdown in a series of subjects such as privatizations, concessions, state reforms, and basic legislation and regulations in the agriculture, water, forestry sectors."
